title: Local network growth: How simple rules drive network complexity
abstract: The Internet, a living cell, a circle of friends, a billion-dollar construction project: these systems share almost nothing -- yet, drawn as networks, they look astonishingly alike. Each has a few giant hubs among a multitude of sparsely connected nodes, short paths between any two parts, dense local clustering, communities, and many redundant routes. For two decades such patterns have been credited to "preferential attachment," the rich getting richer -- a rule that, taken literally, asks every newcomer to survey the whole network before it links. This book makes a simpler case, and defends it one mechanism at a time: the global regularities of real networks are not imposed from above but emerge from purely local rules, in which each new node acts only on a node it has reached and that node's immediate neighbours. A surfer following links, a friend introducing a friend, a gene copied with its connections -- none consults the network as a whole, yet each builds, in the aggregate, the full and unmistakable signature of a real complex system. Written for the curious reader as much as the specialist, with the ideas told in plain language and the mathematics set aside in boxes that can be skipped, it shows how citation graphs, the web, social ties, protein interactions, and project schedules all grow themselves from the same handful of local rules -- one local decision at a time.
summary: This work argues that the complex structure of real networks—from social media to the web—does not require a global organizing principle. Instead, these intricate patterns emerge naturally and robustly from simple, localized rules governing how new connections are formed one node at a time.
main_problem: The paper addresses how complex, global statistical regularities found in real-world networks (like the Internet or social graphs) emerge from simple, purely local growth rules rather than requiring a global mechanism like preferential attachment.
main_result: Global network patterns—such as scale-free degree distributions and high clustering—are shown to be emergent consequences of microscopic decisions made only by newly connected nodes interacting with their immediate neighbors.
method: The methodology involves identifying and testing specific local growth rules (e.g., search, triadic closure) against macroscopic network diagnostics using mean-field arguments and comparative analysis with deterministic models.
model_or_system: The study applies to a wide variety of complex networks, including the Internet graph, social ties, protein interaction maps, and project dependency graphs. The focus is on the abstract mathematical structure of connectivity rather than a specific physical Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Degree distribution ($p(k) \sim k^{-\gamma}$), small-world properties (short paths, high clustering), community structure scaling ($\sqrt{n}$ vs $n eta$), and local correlations between neighboring node degrees.
important_parameters: The growth rule itself is the key parameter; variations in this local decision process determine the resulting global exponents and structural metrics.
main_assumptions: The central assumption is that locality dictates globality, meaning complex structure arises from simple, non-global interactions. Early analyses must carefully distinguish between measurement artifacts and true emergent properties.
figures_summary: Not specified; the notes describe conceptual figures illustrating degree counting and structural comparisons (e.g., ring lattice vs. real networks).
paper_structure: The paper builds its argument by first establishing the observed global regularities, then systematically challenging the necessity of global rules, and finally proposing that local mechanisms are sufficient to generate all observed complexity.
why_interesting: While not quantum in nature, the principles of emergent complexity from local interactions resonate with concepts in many-body physics, such as how collective behavior arises from individual particle Hamiltonians or local field interactions.

figures.caption: Figure 1.1: Degree. A node’s degree is simply its number of links. Drawn here with node size growing with degree: a few hubs (such as the central one, k = 7) carry many links, while most nodes have only one or two. That imbalance — many small nodes, a few giant hubs — is the hallmark of a scale-free network.

Figure 1.2: Clustering coefficient. The clustering of the central node (gray) is the fraction of its neighbor pairs that are themselves linked. (a) Four of the six neighbor pairs are linked (the bold links), so c ≈0.67 — a cliquish neighborhood. (b) No neighbors are linked to each other, so c = 0.

Figure 1.3: Distance. The distance between two nodes is the number of links on the shortest route between them. The shortest route from A to B here is three hops (in bold); the lower route is longer. In real networks these shortest distances stay small even as the network grows — the small-world effect.

Figure 1.4: Degree correlations. (a) In an assortative network, hubs tend to link to other hubs (“birds of a feather”). (b) In a disassortative one, hubs avoid each other and link instead to low- degree nodes (“opposites attract”). Social networks lean assortative; technological and biological ones, disassortative.

Figure 1.6: Why the standard clustering coefficient misleads. The hub’s neighbors all have degree two, and each spends its spare link on another neighbor of the hub. They are therefore as intercon- nected as their degrees allow — no rewiring could add a single link among them. Yet the standard coefficient, Eq.
